title: credit_risk_random_forest
text: Lenders want to know, before approving a loan, how likely the borrower is to default. In this tutorial you will predict that with a random forest, which is a crowd of many decision trees that vote on the answer. It is one of three credit risk tutorials that use the same dataset, so you can compare the models fairly at the end: random forest, XGBoost and LightGBM.

title: credit_risk_random_forest
text:
What you need

A place to run code, such as a notebook
A public credit default dataset. Pick one, such as the German Credit dataset or the “Give Me Some Credit” dataset, and use the same one on all three pages.

title: credit_risk_random_forest
text:
Steps

Load the data. Open the dataset and look at the first few rows. Find the column that says whether each borrower defaulted. That is what you are trying to predict.
Check how rare defaults are. Count defaulters against non-defaulters. Defaults are usually a small share, which matters later.
Clean up. Fill or remove missing values, and turn any text columns, such as “owns home” or “rents”, into numbers.
Split the data. Set aside 20% of borrowers for testing and keep their results hidden. Make sure the split keeps the same share of defaulters in both groups.
Train a first forest. Use the default settings and a few hundred trees. A random forest needs no rescaling of the numbers.
Test it. Predict the default chance for the hidden borrowers.
Measure it properly. Do not rely on plain accuracy, because a model that says “nobody defaults” would look excellent when defaults are rare. Use the AUC score instead, which measures how well the model ranks risky borrowers above safe ones.
Tune two settings. Try different numbers of trees and different maximum tree depths. Keep the combination that scores best on a validation slice, not the test set.
See what mattered. Plot the importance of each column. Which facts about a borrower drive the predictions?
Record your result. Write down the test AUC. You will compare it with the other two models.

title: credit_risk_random_forest
text:
What to look for

A forest that scores almost perfectly on the training data but much worse on the test data is memorizing, so limit the tree depth.
Do the important columns make sense to you as reasons someone might default?

title: bonds_1d_cnn
text: A 1D convolutional neural network (CNN) slides a small window along a sequence and learns to spot short patterns in it. In this tutorial you will use one to forecast tomorrow’s change in a Treasury bond yield from its recent history, and you will test whether it beats a simple guess.

title: bonds_1d_cnn
text:
What you need

A place to run code, such as a notebook
Daily 10-year US Treasury yields. The Federal Reserve’s free FRED website offers them as a download.

title: bonds_1d_cnn
text:
Steps

Get the yields. Download about ten years of daily 10-year Treasury yields and put them in date order.
Tidy the data. Remove the days with no value, such as holidays.
Look at the yields. Plot them over time to get a feel for the long swings.
Switch to daily changes. Work out how much the yield moved from each day to the next. Changes are much easier for a model to learn from than the yield level itself.
Build the training examples. Each example is the last 30 days of changes. The answer for that example is the next day’s change.
Split by time. Use the earliest 70% for training, the next 15% for validation, and the most recent 15% for testing. Never shuffle.
Rescale the changes. Work out the scaling from the training period only.
Build a small network. Start with one or two convolution layers followed by a final output layer. Small is fine, and more layers will not necessarily help.
Train it. Watch the error on the training days and on the validation days. Stop when the validation error stops improving.
Score it on the test days. Measure the average size of its mistakes.
Compare with a lazy guess. Check the score against always predicting “no change”. This comparison is the real test.
Plot the forecasts. Draw the predictions next to what actually happened for the test period.

title: bonds_1d_cnn
text:
What to look for

Daily changes in bond yields are hard to forecast. If your network only matches the lazy guess, you have learned something real about how efficient the market is.
Try a shorter and a longer window than 30 days and see whether the result changes.

title: garch
text: Stock prices do not move calmly all the time. Quiet weeks are followed by wild ones, and wild days tend to come in bunches. A GARCH model is a simple tool for capturing that pattern. In this tutorial you will fit one to Fortinet (FTNT) and see how risky the stock looks on any given day.

title: garch
text:
What you need

A place to run code, such as a notebook
FTNT’s daily prices from a free source such as Yahoo Finance

title: garch
text:
Steps

Get the prices. Download about five years of FTNT daily closing prices and put them in date order.
Turn prices into returns. A return is the percentage change from one day to the next.
Look before you model. Plot the returns over time. Notice the stretches where the line is calm and the stretches where it swings wildly. That bunching is called volatility clustering, and it is the whole reason this model exists.
Choose the simplest model. Pick the standard starting version, called GARCH(1,1). It uses just yesterday’s surprise and yesterday’s risk level to estimate today’s.
Fit it. Let your software find the model’s settings from the data. This is usually a single step.
Read the three key results. One is the stock’s usual long-run risk level. Another is how strongly it reacts to a big move. The third is how long the effect of that move lingers. Write down what each means in your own words.
Plot the risk over time. Draw the model’s daily volatility estimate. It should rise after turbulent days and fade during quiet spells.
Look ahead. Ask the model for a forecast of the next few days and see how quickly it settles back to the long-run level.

title: garch
text:
What to look for

Compare the model’s volatility line with a simple 20-day moving measure of the returns’ spread. Which reacts faster?
Do the biggest spikes line up with news events you can recall for the company or the market?

When you are done, continue to VaR to turn volatility into a loss estimate.

title: credit_risk_xgboost
text: Lenders want to know, before approving a loan, how likely the borrower is to default. In this tutorial you will predict that with XGBoost, a method that builds decision trees one after another, where each new tree concentrates on the mistakes the earlier ones made. It is one of three credit risk tutorials that use the same dataset, so you can compare the models fairly at the end: random forest, XGBoost and LightGBM.

title: credit_risk_xgboost
text:
What you need

A place to run code, such as a notebook
The same public credit default dataset you used in the random forest tutorial. If you have not done that one yet, pick a dataset such as German Credit or “Give Me Some Credit”.

title: credit_risk_xgboost
text:
Steps

Load the data. Open the dataset and find the column that says whether each borrower defaulted. That is what you are trying to predict.
Clean up. Handle missing values and turn any text columns into numbers. XGBoost can cope with some gaps in the data, but it is good practice to look at them first.
Split the data. Use the exact same test borrowers as in the other tutorials. Then take a further slice of the training data to use as a validation set.
Train a first model. Use the default settings and a modest number of trees.
Test it. Predict the default chance for the hidden test borrowers and measure the AUC score, which shows how well the model ranks risky borrowers above safe ones.
Use early stopping. Let the model keep adding trees while watching its score on the validation set. Stop when the score stops improving. This is how you avoid memorizing the training data.
Tune three settings. Try changing the learning rate, which is how big a step each new tree takes, the maximum tree depth, and the number of trees. Smaller steps with more trees is usually safer.
See what mattered. Plot the importance of each column.
Record your result. Write down the test AUC for comparison with the other two models.

title: credit_risk_xgboost
text:
What to look for

Boosting is often slightly more accurate than a random forest, but it is also easier to over-tune. Does that match what you see?
Note how long training took. You will compare that with LightGBM.

title: FTNT_lstm_garch_to_var
text: In this tutorial you will forecast how risky Fortinet (FTNT) will be tomorrow by combining two tools: a GARCH model, which tracks volatility, and an LSTM, a neural network that reads a sequence in order and remembers what just happened. Then you will turn the forecast into a Value at Risk (VaR) number and test whether it held up.

title: FTNT_lstm_garch_to_var
text:
What you need

A place to run code, such as a notebook
FTNT’s daily prices from a free source such as Yahoo Finance
Some familiarity with the garch and var tutorials, which cover the basics used here

title: FTNT_lstm_garch_to_var
text:
Steps

Get the prices. Download about seven years of FTNT daily closing prices, since the neural network needs more history than the simpler models.
Turn prices into returns. A return is the percentage change from one day to the next.
Fit a GARCH model. Use the standard GARCH(1,1) and save its daily volatility estimate for every day.
Define the target. For each day, the thing to predict is how large the next day’s move is.
Build the training examples. Each example is a window of the last 20 days. For each of those days, it holds the return and the GARCH volatility. The answer for that window is the next day’s move.
Split by time. Use the earliest 70% for training, the next 15% for validation, and the most recent 15% for testing. Never shuffle.
Rescale the inputs. Work out the scaling from the training period only.
Train the LSTM. Watch the error on the training days and on the validation days as it learns. Stop when the validation error stops improving. If it keeps falling on training days but rises on validation days, the network is memorizing.
Forecast tomorrow’s risk. Run the test period through the trained network to get a risk forecast for each day.
Turn the forecast into VaR. Multiply each day’s forecast by the standard factor for 95% confidence, which is about 1.65, then apply it to an imaginary $10,000 position.
Backtest. Count the days the real loss was worse than the VaR number. At 95% confidence, that should happen on about 5 days out of 100.
Compare. Repeat step 10 using the GARCH forecast alone. Which one had a hit rate closer to 5%?

title: FTNT_lstm_garch_to_var
text:
What to look for

A hit rate far above 5% means the model understates risk. A rate far below means it is too cautious.
The LSTM is a lot more work than GARCH. Decide honestly whether it was worth it for this stock.

title: var
text: Value at Risk (VaR) answers one question: on a bad day, how much could I lose? In this tutorial you will estimate it for Fortinet (FTNT) stock, using nothing but its own price history.

title: var
text:
What you need

A place to run code, such as a notebook
An internet connection to download FTNT’s daily prices

title: var
text:
Steps

Get the prices. Download FTNT’s daily closing prices for roughly the last five years from a free source such as Yahoo Finance.
Tidy the data. Put the rows in date order and remove any days with missing prices.
Turn prices into returns. A return is the percentage change from one day to the next. Returns are easier to compare over time than raw prices, because a $5 move means something different at $50 than at $500.
Choose your settings. Pick a confidence level and a time horizon. A good start is 95% confidence and a one-day horizon. Ninety-five percent confidence means you are looking at the worst 1 day in 20.
Find the cutoff. Line the returns up from worst to best and find the point where the worst 5% ends. That cutoff return is your VaR.
Turn it into dollars. Imagine you hold $10,000 of FTNT and apply the cutoff to that amount.
Draw it. Make a histogram of the daily returns and mark the cutoff with a vertical line, so you can see how much of the history sits beyond it.
Say it in plain words. Finish the sentence: “On 95 days out of 100, I would expect to lose no more than this much.”

title: var
text:
What to look for

Change the confidence level to 99%. The loss estimate gets bigger. Why do you think that is?
This method assumes the future looks like the past. Think about what kind of day would break that assumption.

Next, see how Monte Carlo estimates the same number a different way.

title: monte_carlo
text: A Monte Carlo simulation answers “what could happen?” by playing out thousands of possible futures and looking at the results. In this tutorial you will simulate possible price paths for Fortinet (FTNT) and use them to estimate Value at Risk (VaR), the amount you might lose on a bad day.

title: monte_carlo
text:
What you need

A place to run code, such as a notebook
FTNT’s daily prices from a free source such as Yahoo Finance

title: monte_carlo
text:
Steps

Get the prices. Download about five years of FTNT daily closing prices and put them in date order.
Turn prices into returns. A return is the percentage change from one day to the next.
Measure two things. Work out the stock’s average daily return and how much the returns typically swing around that average. These two numbers describe the “personality” of the stock.
Choose your settings. Decide how many days ahead to simulate (start with 10) and how many simulated futures to run (start with 10,000).
Run the simulation. For each future, draw a random daily return for every day, using the average and swing from step 3, and stack them to build a price path. Repeat until you have all 10,000 paths.
Plot a few paths. Draw about 50 of them on one chart. You should see a fan that spreads out over time.
Look at where the paths end. Make a histogram of the final prices or the total returns.
Find the cutoff. Locate the point where the worst 5% of outcomes begins. That is your 95% VaR, which you can express in dollars for an imaginary $10,000 position.
Check your stability. Run it again. The answer will change slightly each time. Then try 100,000 paths and see how much steadier it gets.

title: monte_carlo
text:
What to look for

Compare your result with the one from the VaR tutorial. Why might they differ?
This simulation assumes returns follow a smooth bell shape. Real markets have more extreme days than that, so think about which way the estimate is probably wrong.

title: Testing SMA Trading Strategy - 2016 to 2026
text:
This project was inspired by Professor Yi Tang at Fordham University, Gabelli School of Business as part of my Investment Applications class.
Professor Tang introduced the findings of Faber and showed that a SMA strategy outperformed buying and holding prior to 2016. Now that we are in a new decade though, it seems worthwhile to test if this strategy still holds, and if not, why not?
(It also acts as a good way to practice python and get out of R-world)
The Results: –> Buy and hold had higher total returns in both tests –> SMA had less volatility, smaller max drawdowns, and higher Sharpe ratios –> The pattern was consistent across all four window lengths
My takeaway: the SMA rule buys protection from big drops at the cost of some upside. That cost was clear in a decade where US stocks mostly rose.
Possible issues: Abnormal decade with mostly positive sp500 returns, cash is not re-invested into short term bonds, I replaced Faber’s indices with ETFs (because I’m not willing to pay for that data).

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import yfinance as yf
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt


START_DATE = "2016-01-01"
END_DATE = "2026-01-01"


SP500 = "SPY"
GAA = {"SPY":"US Stocks", "EFA":"Foreign Stocks", "IEF":"10yr Bonds", "VNQ":"REIT", "GSG":"Commodities"}
FUNDS = 0.0


def get_prices():
  tickers = sorted(set([SP500, *GAA]))
  daily = yf.download(tickers, start = START_DATE, end = END_DATE, auto_adjust = True, progress = False)["Close"]
  group_by_month = daily.resample("ME")
  monthly = group_by_month.last().dropna(how="all")
  return monthly


def sma_strategy(prices, assets, months):
  returns = prices.pct_change()
  sma = prices[assets].rolling(months).mean()
  above_sma = prices[assets] > sma
  in_market = above_sma.shift(1, fill_value = False)
  sma_ready = sma.notna().shift(1, fill_value = False)
  cash_returns = pd.DataFrame(FUNDS, index = returns.index, columns = assets)
  asset_returns = returns[assets].where(in_market, cash_returns)
  asset_returns = asset_returns.where(sma_ready)
  portfolio = asset_returns.mean(axis = 1, skipna = False)
  return portfolio.dropna()


def buy_and_hold(prices, assets):
    return prices.pct_change()[assets].mean(axis=1)


def stats(returns):
  years = len(returns) / 12
  growth = (1 + returns).prod()
  curve = (1 + returns).cumprod()
  total_return = growth - 1
  cagr = growth ** (1 / years) - 1
  volatility = returns.std() * np.sqrt(12)
  sharpe = returns.mean() / returns.std() * np.sqrt(12)
  drawdown = curve / curve.cummax() - 1
  max_drawdown = drawdown.min()
  worst_month = returns.min()
  return {"Total return":total_return, "CAGR":cagr, "Volatility":volatility, "Sharpe":sharpe, "Max drawdown":max_drawdown, "Worst month":worst_month}


def show(title, series):
  start = max(returns.index[0] for returns in series.values())
  window = {name: returns.loc[start:] for name, returns in series.items()}
  end = max(returns.index[-1] for returns in window.values())
  table = pd.DataFrame({name: stats(returns) for name, returns in window.items()}).T
  formatted = table.copy()
  for column in formatted.columns:
    if column == "Sharpe":
      formatted[column] = table[column].map(lambda x: f"{x:7.2f}")
    else:
      formatted[column] = table[column].map(lambda x: f"{x:7.1%}")
  print(f"\n=== {title} ===")
  print(f"(compared over {start:%Y-%m} to {end:%Y-%m})")
  print(formatted.to_string())
  return window


def main():
  prices = get_prices()
  print(f"Data: {prices.index[0]:%Y-%m} to {prices.index[-1]:%Y-%m}  (test window starts {START_DATE[:7]})")
  print("Note: the latest month may be incomplete if run before month-end.")

  # Test 1: S&P 500 vs SMA(10)
  sp500_buy_and_hold = buy_and_hold(prices, [SP500])
  sp500_sma = sma_strategy(prices, [SP500], 10)
  test_1 = {"S&P 500 buy & hold": sp500_buy_and_hold, "S&P 500 + 10m SMA": sp500_sma}
  window_1 = show("Test 1: S&P 500 vs 10-month SMA", test_1)

  # Test 2: GAA vs SMA(10)
  assets = list(GAA)
  gaa_buy_and_hold = buy_and_hold(prices, assets)
  gaa_sma = sma_strategy(prices, assets, 10)
  test_2 = {"GAA buy & hold": gaa_buy_and_hold, "GAA + 10m SMA": gaa_sma}
  window_2 = show("Test 2: 5-asset GAA vs 10-month SMA", test_2)

  # Test 3: GAA with different SMA lengths
  test_3 = {"GAA buy & hold": gaa_buy_and_hold}
  for months in (6, 8, 10, 12):
    test_3[f"GAA + {months}m SMA"] = sma_strategy(prices, assets, months)
  window_3 = show("Test 3: GAA with 6, 8, 10, 12-month SMA", test_3)

  # Chart
  fig, axes = plt.subplots(3, 1, figsize = (8, 12))
  charts = [("Test 1: S&P 500", window_1), ("Test 2: GAA", window_2), ("Test 3: GAA, SMA lengths", window_3)]
  for ax, (chart_title, window) in zip(axes, charts):
    for name, returns in window.items():
      growth_of_100 = (1 + returns).cumprod() * 100
      ax.plot(growth_of_100, label = name)
    ax.set_title(chart_title)
    ax.set_yscale("log")
    ax.set_ylabel("Growth of 100 (log)")
    ax.legend(fontsize = 8)
  fig.tight_layout()
  fig.savefig("sma_results.png", dpi = 150)
  print("\nSaved chart: sma_results.png")


if __name__ == "__main__":
  main()

Data: 2016-01 to 2025-12  (test window starts 2016-01)
Note: the latest month may be incomplete if run before month-end.

title: FTNT_ridge_regression
text: Can recent price moves help predict tomorrow’s return? Ridge regression is a simple prediction method that stays steady when your clues overlap with each other. In this tutorial you will use it on Fortinet (FTNT) stock and, just as importantly, learn how to tell whether it actually helped.

title: FTNT_ridge_regression
text:
What you need

A place to run code, such as a notebook
FTNT’s daily prices from a free source such as Yahoo Finance

title: FTNT_ridge_regression
text:
Steps

Get the prices. Download about five years of FTNT daily closing prices and put them in date order.
Turn prices into returns. A return is the percentage change from one day to the next.
Build the clues. For each day, create a few simple clues from the past: the returns of the last five days, the average return of the last 20 days, and how wild the last 20 days were.
Set the target. The thing you want to predict is the next day’s return. Line each day’s clues up with the following day’s return.
Split by time. Use the earliest 70% of days for training and the most recent 30% for testing. Never shuffle the days, because that would let the model peek at the future.
Put the clues on the same scale. Rescale each clue so none dominates just because its numbers are bigger. Work out the scaling from the training days only.
Fit ridge regression with several penalty strengths. The penalty stops the model from leaning too hard on any one clue. Try a small, a medium and a large one.
Pick the best penalty. Compare them on a validation slice taken from the end of the training period, not the test set.
Score it on the test days. Measure the average size of the model’s mistakes.
Compare with a lazy guess. Check how the model does against always predicting “no change”. This comparison is the real test.

title: FTNT_ridge_regression
text:
What to look for

Daily stock returns are very hard to predict, so expect a result that is only slightly better than the lazy guess, or no better at all. That is a normal finding, not a failure.
Look at the clue weights as the penalty grows. They shrink toward zero. Which clues survive the longest?

title: credit_risk_lightGBM
text: Lenders want to know, before approving a loan, how likely the borrower is to default. In this tutorial you will predict that with LightGBM, a fast cousin of XGBoost that also builds trees one after another, each learning from the last one’s mistakes. It is one of three credit risk tutorials that use the same dataset, so you can compare the models fairly at the end: random forest, XGBoost and LightGBM.

title: credit_risk_lightGBM
text:
What you need

A place to run code, such as a notebook
The same public credit default dataset you used in the other two credit risk tutorials. If you have not done those yet, pick a dataset such as German Credit or “Give Me Some Credit”.

title: credit_risk_lightGBM
text:
Steps

Load the data. Open the dataset and find the column that says whether each borrower defaulted. That is what you are trying to predict.
Clean up. Look at any missing values. LightGBM can handle gaps, and it can also read text categories such as “owns home” or “rents” directly if you mark them as categories.
Split the data. Use the exact same test borrowers as in the other tutorials, plus a validation slice taken from the training data.
Train a first model. Use the default settings.
Test it. Predict the default chance for the hidden test borrowers and measure the AUC score, which shows how well the model ranks risky borrowers above safe ones.
Use early stopping. Watch the score on the validation set while the model adds trees, and stop when it stops improving.
Tune three settings. Try the number of leaves, which controls how complex each tree can get, the learning rate, and the minimum number of borrowers allowed in a leaf. If your data is small, keep the number of leaves low.
See what mattered. Plot the importance of each column.
Record your result. Write down the test AUC and the training time.
Compare all three. Make a small table with the AUC and the training time for the random forest, XGBoost and LightGBM.

title: credit_risk_lightGBM
text:
What to look for

On a dataset this small, the three models usually score very close to each other. Be careful about declaring a winner from a tiny difference.
LightGBM’s advantage shows up on large datasets. Does it train noticeably faster here?
